title: Coffee and Cigarettes
full_review:
"Coffee and Cigarettes" (United Artists) is a pell-mell patchwork of short films, loosely held together by a paste of roasted grinds and dried tobacco.

Each of the 11 vignettes involves a pair of actors sitting around, drinking coffee and smoking cigarettes while conversing on such eclectic subjects as Paris in the1920s, Elvis conspiracies and the inventions of Nikola Telsa -- which sounds more interesting than it really is.

The oddball assortment of sketches, shot in black-and-white over the past 17 years by maverick filmmaker Jim Jarmusch, ranges from the mildly amusing to the utterly inane.

The opening installment, "Strange to Meet You," premiered in 1986 on "Saturday Night Live" and revolves around two "wound-up" caffeine junkies (Roberto Benigni and Steven Wright), who discuss getting children hooked early on "caffeine pops" and the merits of drinking coffee before bedtime -- one benefit being you can dream at Indy-500 speed.

Actors and musicians, including Bill Murray, Steve Buscemi, Iggy Pop and Tom Waits, play themselves in several of the minimovies. In one, entitled "Somewhere in California," Pop and Waits unwind while chewing the fat about roadside surgery and self-delusional post-chain-smoking bliss.

Ironically enough, the two most wryly witty vignettes share almost identical titles. In "Cousins," Cate Blanchett, in addition to playing herself, also dons a dark wig as her less-successful cousin, Shelly, whose thinly veiled jealousy leads to a tense tete-a-tete during a break at a movie press junket in a ritzy hotel suite. In "Cousins?" Alfred Molina and Steve Coogan, both playing themselves, use a surprise genealogical discovery to lampoon Hollywood superficiality.
At the other end of the spectrum is "Renee," an insipid installment about a woman (Renee French) whose magazine browsing keeps getting interrupted by unsolicited coffee refills.
In addition to the cup-of-joe connection, the loosely linked collage uses visual motifs such as overhead shots and checkered tabletops to unify the larger piece.

Though Jarmusch's patchwork approach is interesting, the net result is neither as developed nor as entertaining as his similar slice-of-life "Night on Earth" (1992), which knits together five separate stories all set in taxicabs.

And while he once again uses commonplace activities (what's more ho-hum than chatting over some fresh brew?) to explore societal peccadilloes, the smokescreen of social commentary lifts rather quickly, revealing the film for what it is: a motley mosaic of over-caffeinated conversations involving people sitting around talking nicotine-stained nonsense.

In regard to its depiction of smoking, one is never quite sure if the film is celebrating or merely commenting on what is, sadly, a national addiction.

Full of artsy absurdity, this pot of "Coffee" is cinematic decaf, providing only a minimal amount of stimulation.

Due to some rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
